how-much-does-diluted-cleaning-solution-.text:
← Cleaning chemical dilution calculator

How much does one diluted gallon really cost?

A concentrate's sticker price describes the container, not the ready-to-use gallon it ends up making. Dilution ratio, mixing labor, and waste all change what a bucket or a full job actually costs before you ever write a bid.

Open the free dilution cost calculator

What the container price does not tell you

The dilution ratio does the real work. The same $32 gallon of concentrate produces a very different cost per ready-to-use gallon at a 1:32 dilution than at a 1:8 dilution — the label ratio, not the bottle price, sets the per-gallon cost.

Mixing labor is a real, if small, add. A few minutes per batch multiplied across a week of mixing is worth pricing deliberately rather than absorbing silently.

Waste is not zero. Spillage, over-pour, and solution mixed but not used all reduce how much of what you paid for actually reaches a surface.

Worked example

A label calling for 4 fl oz of concentrate per gallon of water, a $32 container holding 128 fl oz, a 5% waste allowance, 3 minutes of mixing labor at a $22 loaded rate, and a 5-gallon bucket:

FigureValue
Concentrate cost per ounce$0.25
Chemical cost for one ready-to-use gallon$1.00
Mixing labor for that batch$1.10
Waste allowance added$0.11
Cost per ready-to-use gallon$2.21
Cost for a 5-gallon bucket$11.05

Use the bucket or job figure in a bid instead of treating cleaning chemical as a flat percentage of the job — a job that fills several buckets a day is spending real dollars that a flat allowance can badly under- or over-state.

Common questions

How do I calculate the cost per gallon of diluted cleaning chemical?

Divide the container price by its size to get a cost per ounce, multiply by the concentrate used per batch to get the chemical cost, add any mixing labor, then divide by the ready-to-use water volume. A $32 gallon container (128 fl oz) diluted at 4 fl oz per gallon of water costs $0.25 per ounce and $1.00 in chemical for that gallon before labor or waste.

Should mixing labor be included in the cost of a cleaning solution?

Yes, if you are pricing a job rather than just restocking chemical. Three minutes at a $22 loaded labor rate adds $1.10 to a batch — small on its own, but it compounds across every bucket mixed in a week and belongs in a bid the same way chemical cost does.

Why does a waste allowance increase the cost per gallon?

A waste allowance spreads unavoidable spillage, over-pour, and dumped unused solution across every gallon that is actually used, rather than pretending none of it happens. A 5% allowance on a batch costing $2.10 in chemical and labor adds about $0.11, landing the real cost per gallon at $2.21 instead of the $2.10 the raw math would show.

Safety: follow the product label and SDS. Never mix chemicals unless the manufacturer explicitly permits it. This page does not determine safe handling, PPE, storage, or compatibility.

Common questions

Why does mixing labor cost more than the chemical itself?

On the default example — a 1:32 dilution from a $32, 128 fl oz container — the concentrate works out to 25¢ an ounce, so 4 fl oz of concentrate costs $1.00. Three minutes of mixing at a $22/hour loaded labor rate costs $1.10. A cheap concentrate does not make a batch cheap if someone spends real minutes mixing it: at a decent wage, labor can be the larger half of what a batch actually costs, and a price built on chemical cost alone undercharges for it.

Why does the waste allowance divide the cost instead of adding a percentage on top?

Because waste describes volume lost, not an extra fee. Dividing by (1 − waste%) grosses the batch cost up so the ready-to-use gallons you actually deliver still cost what they should, even though some of what you mixed never made it out of the bucket, sprayer, or mop. On the default 5% allowance, the $2.10 combined chemical-and-labor cost becomes a $2.21 batch cost — the extra 11¢ is what one batch's worth of spillage and dead space adds back onto the gallons that do get used.

What is the difference between cost per gallon and cost per bucket?

“Ready-to-use water” is how many gallons a single batch of concentrate makes, which is what cost per gallon is measured against. “Bucket or job size” is a separate figure — how many gallons your actual bucket or job uses — and cost per bucket simply scales the per-gallon figure up to that size. Getting the two mixed up under- or over-states a bid by whatever the ratio between them happens to be.

Why does concentrate cost per ounce use container size, not the amount in one batch?

Container price and container size set your unit cost — what one fluid ounce of concentrate costs you, however much of it a single batch uses. “Concentrate per batch” is a different field: how many of those ounces one batch actually mixes in. Changing the batch amount changes chemical cost per batch; it does not change what an ounce costs you to buy.

Are my numbers saved, and can I share them?

Your last entry is saved in this browser's local storage, so refreshing the page or coming back later restores it — nothing is uploaded. “Copy shareable link” puts the same numbers in the page's URL fragment (after the #) instead, so sending that link to a coworker or supplier opens this page with the exact same job priced, without either of you retyping anything. A link takes priority over a saved draft when you open one.

This calculator vs. Janitorial Manager

Two different shapes: Janitorial Manager is an account-based platform for running a cleaning company's bidding, inspections, and work orders. This page is a free, private worksheet for one narrower question — what does the ready-to-use gallon I am about to pour actually cost — before that number becomes a line in a bid.

What each tool is for

Janitorial Manager is a cloud-based janitorial business management platform, described on its own site as covering bidding, inspections, work order management, and staff and supply tracking for commercial cleaning companies. It is an account-based platform: a cleaning company signs up and runs its bidding, inspections, and day-to-day operations through it as an ongoing subscription, not a one-off calculator. Janitorial Manager's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — janitorial business management software with a bidding module, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Janitorial Manager appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Janitorial Manager does. It does not bid a whole job, schedule inspections, manage work orders, or store a customer or staff record on a server. It takes the concentrate ratio printed on the product label, the container's price and size, the bucket or job size you need, and optional mixing labor minutes and a waste allowance, and turns that into the cost per ready-to-use gallon, per bucket, and per job — plus, since concentrate is only sold in whole containers, how many containers a job actually needs to buy, the real purchase cost of those containers, and how much concentrate is left over for the next job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Janitorial Manager?

They do different jobs, and a janitorial or commercial cleaning company of any size may end up touching both. Janitorial Manager is a cloud-based, account-based janitorial business management platform used to bid jobs, run inspections, manage work orders, and track staff and supplies across a cleaning operation, sold as an ongoing subscription. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from the concentrate ratio on the product label, the supplier's container price, and optional mixing labor and a waste allowance, it turns that into the cost per ready-to-use gallon, per bucket, and per job, plus how many whole containers of concentrate a job actually needs to buy and what is left over. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A company that already bids, inspects, and dispatches through one system is better served by Janitorial Manager or a comparable janitorial management platform; someone who wants an instant, private answer to what a diluted gallon costs before that figure goes into a bid line is in the right place here.

Does this calculator help me price a whole janitorial bid, not just the chemical?

No. It prices one input to a bid — the ready-to-use cost of a diluted cleaning chemical, including mixing labor and a waste allowance — not labor hours for the whole job, square footage, frequency, supplies beyond the chemical itself, or overhead and margin on the full contract. Those still belong in a full bid or in janitorial bidding software built for that job. This tool answers the narrower question a flat percentage for "chemical cost" usually gets wrong.

vs-pricing-off-the-label-price.html.text:
← Cleaning Chemical Dilution Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. pricing off the label price

The concentrate label prices the chemical. It has no field for the minutes someone spends mixing it, or the ounces that never make it out of the bucket — and both are real costs a job still has to cover.

What pricing off the label price is

It is the fast way to answer "what does this cost": take the container's price and size, divide for a cost per ounce, and scale that by the label's dilution ratio to get a price per ready-to-use gallon or bucket. It needs no stopwatch and no separate line for waste, which is exactly why it is the default habit — the label already has the ratio printed on it, so the arithmetic feels complete.

It prices the chemical correctly. It does not price the batch, because mixing labor and any spillage or dead space in the bucket or sprayer never enter that arithmetic anywhere.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the concentrate ratio from the label, the container's price and size, the bucket or job size, optional mixing minutes and a loaded labor rate, and a waste allowance for what does not make it out of the bucket. It returns the ready-to-use cost per gallon and per bucket or job — chemical, labor, and waste together — plus how many whole containers of concentrate the job actually needs to buy.

What pricing off the label doesWhat this calculator does instead
Prices the chemical from the label's dilution ratio and container price, and stops there. Adds mixing labor from the minutes and loaded rate you enter, and a waste allowance for what never reaches the job, on top of the same chemical arithmetic.
On the default example — a $32, 128 fl oz container at 1:32, 3 minutes of mixing at $22/hour, 5% waste, a 5-gallon job — the label-only chemical cost comes to $5.00. This calculator's ready-to-use cost for the same job is about $11.05 — more than double the label-only figure, because labor and waste are real costs the label price has nowhere to put.
Treats a fast, careful mix and a slow, sloppy one as the same price, because neither shows up in the label's ratio. Prices the minutes and the spillage you actually enter, so a slower mix or a wetter job site changes the number instead of disappearing into it.
Gives a per-ounce or per-gallon rate to reuse across jobs by memory. Also reports how many whole containers of concentrate the job needs to buy and what is left over, since concentrate only comes in whole containers and a job's usable gallons rarely divide evenly into them.

Pricing off the label price is not wrong about the chemical — it is silent about labor and waste, and a bid built only on the label price is short by whatever those two actually cost on the job. This calculator does not know your market rate; it replaces the arithmetic the label price leaves out.

Common questions

What does it mean to price off the label price?

Taking the concentrate's container price and size, dividing to get a cost per ounce, and using that figure — scaled by the label's dilution ratio — as the price of the ready-to-use gallon. It answers what the chemical itself costs. It does not answer what the batch costs, because mixing labor and any waste allowance are not in that arithmetic anywhere.

How far off is pricing from the label alone?

On this calculator's own default example — a 1:32 dilution from a $32, 128 fl oz container, 3 minutes of mixing at a $22/hour loaded labor rate, and a 5% waste allowance — the label-only chemical cost for a 5-gallon job comes to $5.00. This calculator's ready-to-use cost for the same job is about $11.05, once mixing labor and waste are counted. The label price alone is less than half the real cost of that job.

Why does mixing labor change the price so much?

Because it is a real cost the label price has no field for. On the default example, 4 fl oz of concentrate costs $1.00 by the label, and three minutes of mixing at $22/hour loaded labor costs $1.10 — more than the chemical itself. A cheap concentrate does not make a batch cheap if someone spends real minutes mixing it.

Why does the waste allowance matter too?

Because it describes volume that is mixed but never delivered — spillage, dead space in a sprayer or mop bucket, the last inch nobody pours out. The label price assumes every ounce mixed reaches the job; a waste allowance grosses the batch cost up so the gallons that actually get used still cover what the whole batch cost to make.

Is pricing off the label ever close enough?

For a very fast, low-labor mix with negligible spillage, the gap can be small. The risk is that the label price cannot tell you when that is true — it looks identical whether mixing took thirty seconds or five minutes, and whether the bucket was topped off precisely or slopped over twice.

Does this calculator know my local labor rate or supplier price?

No. It has no data on wages, supplier pricing, or waste rates in your market. It takes the container price, dilution ratio, mixing minutes, labor rate, and waste allowance you enter and turns them into a ready-to-use cost — the arithmetic the label price alone skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that pricing off the label price is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until mixing labor or waste on a given job stops being negligible. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $5.00 and $11.05 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on its own default example, matching the worked example already published on the calculator's own page, not a claim about any specific operator's real costs.
